questions.q: What are the main layers of Flask's source code and how do they build on each other?
facts: src/flask/sansio holds IO-free base code meant to be reusable by other implementations such as Quart; it must not do IO or use the Flask globals

sansio.scaffold.Scaffold is the common base of the app and of blueprints: it owns the registries (view_functions, error_handler_spec, before/after/teardown functions, context processors, URL processors) and the decorators that fill them
app.py's Flask builds on sansio.app.App and adds the WSGI/request side, importing ctx.AppContext, the globals, sessions, templating, wrappers and cli
blueprints.py's Blueprint subclasses the sansio Blueprint to add static-file serving and a Click command group (cli.AppGroup)

questions.q: What happens end to end when an HTTP request reaches a Flask app?
facts: wsgi_app creates a new AppContext from the WSGI environ for every request (it does not reuse an already-pushed context), pushes it, and pops it in a finally block, passing along the unhandled error if there was one
AppContext.push sets the _cv_app ContextVar, sends appcontext_pushed, opens the session, then matches the URL; a routing failure is stored on request.routing_exception instead of being raised

full_dispatch_request sends request_started and runs preprocess_request (URL value preprocessors, then before_request functions, where a non-None return replaces the view); dispatch_request then raises any stored routing exception or calls view_functions[rule.endpoint](**view_args) through ensure_sync
Exceptions from the hooks or the view go to handle_user_exception, and the result goes to finalize_request, which runs make_response and process_response and sends request_finished

process_response runs after_this_request callbacks first, then after_request functions (innermost blueprint first, app last, each in reverse registration order), then saves the session unless it is a null session

questions.q: What happens when an app developer calls app.register_blueprint(bp, url_prefix=...)?
facts: Decorators on a Blueprint never touch an app: add_url_rule (and route) only record a deferred function, and the app_* hooks use record_once

register_blueprint calls Blueprint.register, which builds the dotted name from name_prefix and the name option, raises ValueError if that name is already in app.blueprints, stores it, and creates a BlueprintSetupState from the options and blueprint defaults

register merges the blueprint's registries (error handlers, request hooks, URL processors, context processors) into the app keyed by the dotted name, then calls every deferred function with the setup state
BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule joins url_prefix and the rule, merges url_defaults, and registers the rule on the app with endpoint "{name_prefix}.{name}.{endpoint}"
Child blueprints are then registered recursively, with url_prefix and subdomain combined with the parent's and name_prefix set to the parent's dotted name

questions.q: Where is session data stored, what does it look like on the wire, and which code reads and writes it?
facts: The default SecureCookieSessionInterface keeps the whole session in one cookie, signed (not encrypted) by an itsdangerous URLSafeTimedSerializer over SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS plus SECRET_KEY (appended last as the current key) and serialized with the tagged JSON serializer; with no secret key open_session returns None
open_session returns an empty session when the cookie is missing, the signature is bad, or it is older than PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME, which is used as max_age for every session, permanent or not
The session is opened by AppContext._get_session (called from push for request contexts), which falls back to make_null_session; reading it through the context's session property sets accessed

Flask.process_response calls save_session, which adds Vary: Cookie if the session was accessed, deletes the cookie when a modified session is now empty, and otherwise writes it only if should_set_cookie: modified, or permanent with SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST

questions.q: Where do flashed messages live between requests, and which code writes and reads them?
facts: flash() appends a (category, message) tuple to session["_flashes"], reassigning the list instead of mutating it in place so session backends with external storage see the change, and sends message_flashed
get_flashed_messages() pops _flashes from the session on its first call in a request and caches the list on the context (app_ctx._flashes), so later calls in the same request return the same messages
Because they live in the session, the default backend stores them in the signed cookie, and without a SECRET_KEY the NullSession makes flash() raise RuntimeError
get_flashed_messages is added to the Jinja globals in create_jinja_environment, so templates can call it directly

questions.q: Where is the code that decides which error handler runs for an exception raised during a request?
facts: App._find_error_handler in sansio/app.py looks handlers up in error_handler_spec, shaped {scope: {code: {exception class: handler}}}, where scope None is the app and otherwise a blueprint name

Search order: handlers for the specific HTTP code before class-only (code None) handlers; within each, the request's blueprints innermost first and then the app; within a scope, the exception's MRO from the most specific class up
errorhandler/register_error_handler store into error_handler_spec[None][code][class]; an int is converted to Werkzeug's exception class for that code (unknown codes raise ValueError)

Blueprint handlers are copied into the app's error_handler_spec under the blueprint's dotted name at registration, and handle_http_exception never consults handlers for RoutingExceptions or code-less HTTPExceptions

questions.q: When a view raises, where is it decided whether the error becomes a handler's response, a 500 page, or propagates out to the server or test?
facts: full_dispatch_request catches any Exception raised by before_request functions or the view and passes it to handle_user_exception

HTTPExceptions go to handle_http_exception unless trap_http_exception traps them (TRAP_HTTP_EXCEPTIONS; TRAP_BAD_REQUEST_ERRORS for any BadRequest; or, when that is unset, BadRequestKeyError in debug mode); other exceptions with no matching handler are re-raised

wsgi_app catches the re-raised exception and calls handle_exception, which sends got_request_exception and re-raises if PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS is true (its default None means testing or debug); otherwise it logs the error and returns a 500, using any InternalServerError handler, which receives InternalServerError(original_exception=e)

Errors raised while finalizing a normal response (for example in after_request functions) propagate out and end up in handle_exception; while finalizing that 500 response (from_error_handler=True) they are only logged

questions.q: Where is the Host header checked against an allow-list, and at what point in a request do a bad host or an unknown URL actually get rejected?
facts: TRUSTED_HOSTS (default None, meaning no check) is applied in create_url_adapter, which sets request.trusted_hosts and calls Werkzeug's get_host; an untrusted host raises SecurityError, a 400 BadRequest
create_url_adapter runs inside AppContext.__init__, which catches the HTTPException and stores it as request.routing_exception; the URL adapter stays None, so no URL matching happens
URL matching (match_request, run during push) stores 404/405/redirect exceptions on request.routing_exception the same way instead of raising them

Stored routing exceptions are raised only in dispatch_request, which runs after preprocess_request, so app-level before_request functions still run for bad-host and unknown-URL requests (request.endpoint is None and request.blueprints is empty, so blueprint hooks do not)

questions.q: What stops someone from registering routes or hooks after the app has started serving, and does that guard cover everything?
facts: Registration methods on apps and blueprints (route, add_url_rule, before_request, errorhandler, register_blueprint, template_filter, teardown_appcontext and others) are wrapped by @setupmethod, which calls _check_setup_finished first
On the app it raises AssertionError once _got_first_request is True; full_dispatch_request sets that flag when the first request is dispatched
On a blueprint it raises once that blueprint has been registered on an app (_got_registered_once, set in register), whether or not any request has been served

Only those method calls are guarded: changing registries such as app.view_functions or app.url_map directly is not checked, and app.run() resets _got_first_request to False when the development server exits

questions.q: Which type represents the current request's context, and how does it relate to the application context?
facts: Since Flask 3.2 one class, ctx.AppContext, represents both; RequestContext survives only as a deprecated alias returned by ctx.__getattr__, and flask.globals.request_ctx likewise returns app_ctx with a warning
An AppContext is a 'request context' when it was created with request data (has_request is True); app.app_context() creates one without a request
Each context owns its own g (an instance of app.app_ctx_globals_class, _AppCtxGlobals by default), url_adapter, request, session, flashed messages and after_this_request callbacks
current_app, g, request, session and app_ctx are all LocalProxy objects over the single ContextVar _cv_app, each reading an attribute of the active AppContext

questions.q: What exactly is an 'endpoint' in Flask, and how do blueprint names show up in it?
facts: An endpoint is the name a URL rule is registered under; it keys view_functions and defaults to the view function's __name__

Blueprint routes are registered on the app with endpoint "{name_prefix}.{name}.{endpoint}" (leading dot stripped), so a nested blueprint's view becomes parent.child.view; name is the registered name, which the name= option can change
request.endpoint is url_rule.endpoint; request.blueprint is the part before the last dot, and request.blueprints lists it and each parent, innermost first
In url_for, an endpoint starting with '.' is relative: during a request it is prefixed with the current blueprint's name, or the dot is dropped when the request is not in a blueprint

questions.q: If I change how the app context is pushed (AppContext.push), what else is affected?
facts: Every request goes through it: wsgi_app builds a new context and calls ctx.push() before dispatch, and in its finally block hands the context to werkzeug.debug.preserve_context, if present, before popping it

push does more than set the ContextVar: it sends appcontext_pushed, opens the session through the session interface, then runs URL matching, so session interfaces and URL converters run inside it and converters can already use the session

Pushes are re-entrant: a push of an already-active context only bumps _push_count, and teardown runs only when the count returns to zero; stream_with_context relies on this, doing 'with ctx:' on the active context so teardown waits until the streamed response finishes
The test client, used as 'with client:', collects preserved contexts and re-pushes them after the response, so push runs again for the same context and teardown runs again when it is finally popped

questions.q: If I change Request.blueprints (the current blueprint and its parents), what is affected?
facts: It is derived from the endpoint: request.blueprint is the endpoint before its last dot, and _split_blueprint_path turns 'a.b' into ['a.b', 'a'], innermost first; it is empty when there is no blueprint or routing failed
preprocess_request iterates (None, *reversed(blueprints)), app first and then outermost to innermost blueprint, for URL value preprocessors and before_request functions
process_response and do_teardown_request iterate chain(blueprints, (None,)), innermost blueprint first and app last
Error-handler lookup (_find_error_handler, called with ctx.request.blueprints) tries blueprint scopes innermost first before the app's

questions.q: How do I add a custom `flask` command for my app or a blueprint, and how does it get an app context?
facts: Flask.__init__ gives every app a cli attribute, an AppGroup named after the app; decorate a function with @app.cli.command() (a flask.Blueprint has its own bp.cli)

AppGroup.command wraps the callback in with_appcontext unless with_appcontext=False is passed, and FlaskGroup.get_command loads the app (ScriptInfo.load_app) and pushes app.app_context() before looking the command up in app.cli
Built-in commands and plugin commands from the flask.commands entry-point group are looked up first, so they still work when the app cannot be loaded

A blueprint's commands are attached when it is registered: by default as a subgroup named after the blueprint's registered name, merged into the top level with cli_group=None, or under a custom name with cli_group='...'

questions.q: How would I let the session cookie store a new Python type beyond the ones Flask already supports?
facts: Session data is serialized by TaggedJSONSerializer; for a new type, subclass flask.json.tag.JSONTag with a unique key and implement check, to_json and to_python

Register it with app.session_interface.serializer.register(MyTag, index=...): tag() uses the first tag in order whose check matches, so index can put a more specific tag ahead of an existing one such as the dict tag; a duplicate key raises KeyError unless force=True
On load, untag converts only a dict with exactly one key that is a registered tag; anything else is left as-is

The serializer is the module-level session_json_serializer, a class attribute of SecureCookieSessionInterface, and Flask.session_interface is itself a class-level instance, so a registered tag applies to every app in the process that uses the default session interface

questions.q: If I add a new built-in configuration key to Flask, where does its default go and how should the code read it?
facts: Built-in keys and their defaults are listed in Flask.default_config in app.py

App.make_config copies default_config into a new config_class (Config, a dict subclass) when the app is constructed, overriding DEBUG from the FLASK_DEBUG environment variable via get_debug_flag(), and rooted at the instance folder if instance_relative_config
Code reads keys directly with self.config["KEY"], or current_app.config["KEY"] in request-side code, as Request.max_content_length does after checking for a per-request override

For attribute access, add a ConfigAttribute("KEY") descriptor on the app class, as done for testing, secret_key and permanent_session_lifetime; it reads and writes through app.config, with an optional get_converter
